verses.zh: （大卫与两河间的亚兰并琐巴的亚兰争战的时候，约押转回，在盐谷攻击以东，杀了一万二千人。那时，大卫作这金诗叫人学习，交与伶长。调用为证的百合花。）　神啊，你丢弃了我们，使我们破败；你向我们发怒，求你使我们复兴！
verses.en: For the music director, according to the shushan-eduth style;[NOTE:1] a prayer[NOTE:2] of David written to instruct others.[NOTE:3] It was written when he fought against Aram Naharaim and Aram Zobah. That was when Joab turned back and struck down[NOTE:4] 12,000 Edomites[NOTE:5] in the Valley of Salt.[NOTE:6] O God, you have rejected us.[NOTE:7] You suddenly turned on us in your anger.[NOTE:8] Please restore us![NOTE:9]
notes: Psalm 60. The psalmist grieves over Israel’s humiliation, but in response to God’s assuring word, he asks for divine help in battle and expresses his confidence in victory.
The Hebrew expression means “lily of the testimony.” It may refer to a particular music style or to a tune title.
The precise meaning of the Hebrew word מִכְתָּם (miktam), which also appears in the heading to Pss 16, 56-59, is uncertain. HALOT 582-83 s.v. defines it as “inscription.”
Heb “to teach.”
In Josh 8:21 and Judg 20:48 the two verbs “turn back” and “strike down” are also juxtaposed. There they refer to a military counter-attack.
Heb “12,000 of Edom.” Perhaps one should read אֲרַם (’aram, “Aram”) here rather than אֱדוֹם (’edom, “Edom”).
The heading apparently refers to the military campaign recorded in 2 Sam 10 and 1 Chr 19.
You have rejected us. See Pss 43:2; 44:9, 23.
Heb “you broke out upon us, you were angry.”

verses.zh: 你使地震动，而且崩裂；求你将裂口医好，因为地摇动。
verses.en: You made the earth quake; you split it open.[NOTE:1] Repair its breaches, for it is ready to fall.[NOTE:2]
notes: The imperfect verbal form here expresses the psalmist’s wish or prayer.

The verb פָּצַם (patsam, “split open”) occurs only here in the OT. An Arabic cognate means “crack,” and an Aramaic cognate is used in Tg. Jer 22:14 with the meaning “break open, frame.” See BDB 822 s.v. and Jastrow 1205 s.v. פְּצַם.sn You made the earth quake; you split it open. The psalmist uses the imagery of an earthquake to describe the nation’s defeat.

verses.zh: 你叫你的民遇见艰难；你叫我们喝那使人东倒西歪的酒。
verses.en: You have made your people experience hard times;[NOTE:1] you have made us drink intoxicating wine.[NOTE:2]
notes: It is ready to fall. The earth is compared to a wall that has been broken by the force of the earthquake (note the preceding line) and is ready to collapse.
Heb “you have caused your people to see [what is] hard.”

verses.zh: 你把旌旗赐给敬畏你的人，可以为真理扬起来。（细拉）
verses.en: You have given your loyal followers[NOTE:1] a rallying flag,so that they might seek safety from the bow.[NOTE:2] (Selah)
notes: Heb “wine of staggering,” that is, intoxicating wine that makes one stagger in drunkenness. Intoxicating wine is here an image of divine judgment that makes its victims stagger like drunkards. See Isa 51:17-23.
Heb “those who fear you.”

verses.zh: 求你应允我们，用右手拯救我们，好叫你所亲爱的人得救。
verses.en: Deliver by your power[NOTE:1] and answer me,[NOTE:2] so that the ones you love may be safe.[NOTE:3]
notes: There is a ray of hope in that God has allowed his loyal followers to rally under a battle flag. The translation assumes the verb is from the root נוּס (nus, “flee”) used here in the Hitpolel in the sense of “find safety for oneself” (HALOT 681 s.v. נוס) or “take flight for oneself” (BDB 630-31 s.v. נוּס). Another option is to take the verb as a denominative from נֵס (nes, “flag”) and translate “that it may be displayed” (BDB 651 s.v. II נסס) or “that they may assemble under the banner” (HALOT 704 s.v. II נסס). Here קֹשֶׁט (qoshet) is taken as an Aramaized form of קֶשֶׁת (qeshet, “bow”; BDB 905-6 s.v. קֶשֶׁת), though some understand the homonymic קֹשְׁטְ (qoshet, “truth”) here (see Prov 22:21; cf. NASB). If one follows the latter interpretation, the line may be translated, “so that they might assemble under the banner for the sake of truth.”
Heb “right hand.”
The Qere (marginal reading) has “me,” while the Kethib (consonantal text) has “us.”

verses.zh: 神已经指着他的圣洁说（说：或译应许我）：我要欢乐；我要分开示剑，丈量疏割谷。
verses.en: God has spoken in his sanctuary:[NOTE:1] “I will triumph. I will parcel out Shechem;the Valley of Sukkoth I will measure off.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “may be rescued.” The lines are actually reversed in the Hebrew text, “So that the ones you love may be rescued, deliver by your power and answer me.”
Heb “in his holy place.”

verses.zh: 基列是我的，玛拿西也是我的。以法莲是护卫我头的；犹大是我的杖。
verses.en: Gilead belongs to me,as does Manasseh.[NOTE:1] Ephraim is my helmet,[NOTE:2] Judah my royal scepter.[NOTE:3]
notes: Shechem stands for the territory west of the Jordan, the Valley of Sukkoth for the region east of the Jordan.
Gilead was located east of the Jordan. Half of the tribe of Manasseh lived east of the Jordan in the region of Bashan.

Heb “the protection of my head.”sn Ephraim, named after one of Joseph’s sons, was one of two major tribes located west of the Jordan. By comparing Ephraim to a helmet, the Lord suggests that the Ephraimites played a primary role in the defense of his land.

verses.zh: 摩押是我的沐浴盆；我要向以东抛鞋。非利士啊，你还能因我欢呼吗？
verses.en: Moab is my washbasin.[NOTE:1] I will make Edom serve me.[NOTE:2] I will shout in triumph over Philistia.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Judah, like Ephraim, was the other major tribe west of the Jordan. The Davidic king, symbolized here by the royal scepter, came from this tribe.
The metaphor of the washbasin, used to rinse one’s hands and feet, suggests that Moab, in contrast to Israel’s elevated position (vv. 6-7), would be reduced to the status of a servant.

Heb “over Edom I will throw my sandal.” The point of the metaphor is not entirely clear. Some interpret this as idiomatic for “taking possession of,” i.e., “I will take possession of Edom.” Others translate עַל (ʿal) as “to” and understand this as referring to a master throwing his dirty sandal to a servant so that the latter might dust it off.

verses.zh: 谁能领我进坚固城？谁能引我到以东地？
verses.en: Who will lead me into the fortified city?Who will bring me to Edom?[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “over me, O Philistia, shout in triumph.” The translation follows the text of Ps 108:9. When the initial עֲלֵיוֹ (ʿaleyo, “over”) was misread as עָלַי (ʿalay, “over me”), the first person verb form was probably altered to an imperative to provide better sense to the line.

verses.zh: 神啊，你不是丢弃了我们吗？　神啊，你不和我们的军兵同去吗？
verses.en: Have you not rejected us, O God?O God, you do not go into battle with our armies.

verses.zh: 求你帮助我们攻击敌人，因为人的帮助是枉然的。
verses.en: Give us help against the enemy,for any help men might offer is futile.[NOTE:1]
notes: In v. 9 the psalmist speaks again and acknowledges his need for help in battle. He hopes God will volunteer, based on the affirmation of sovereignty over Edom in v. 8, but he is also aware that God has seemingly rejected the nation (v. 10, see also v. 1).

verses.zh: 我们倚靠　神才得施展大能，因为践踏我们敌人的就是他。
verses.en: By God’s power we will conquer;[NOTE:1] he will trample down[NOTE:2] our enemies.
notes: Heb “and futile [is] the deliverance of man.”
Heb “in God we will accomplish strength.” The statement refers here to military success (see Num 24:18; 1 Sam 14:48; Pss 108:13; 118:15-16).

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: PSALM 60:1-5
1O
God, You have rejected us. You have broken us;
You have been angry; O, restore us.
2You have made the land
quake, You have split it open;
Heal
its breaches, for it totters.
3You
have made Your people experience hardship;
You have given us wine to drink that
makes us stagger.
4You
have given a banner to those who fear You,
That it may be displayed because of
the truth. Selah.
5That Your beloved may be delivered,
Save with Your right hand, and
answer us!

60:1-3 This strophe describes how the psalmist perceives his/Israel's relationship with YHWH.

- He has rejected us – BDB 276, KB 276, Qal PERFECT, cf. Ps. 44:9,23;
74:1; 77:7; 108:11

- He has broken us – BDB 829, KB 971, Qal PERFECT, possibly related
to a breach in a defensive wall

- He has been angry – BDB 60, KB 72, Qal PERFECT

- He has made their land quake – BDB 950, KB 1271, Hiphil PERFECT

- He has made the land split open – BDB 822, KB 954, Qal PERFECT,
rare word, only here and a related form (i.e., Arabic root) in Jer. 22:14, where it is translated
"cut out" or "break open"

- He made His people experience hardship – BDB 906, KB 1157, Hiphil
PERFECT

- He gave them wine to drink (i.e., cause drunkenness and staggering) – BDB 1052, KB 1639,
Hiphil PERFECT, the cup might be for the nations (cf. Jer. 25:16-26), is
now given to the covenant people with the same effect (cf. Isa. 51:17,22)

Notice that all the VERBS are PERFECTS, which denotes a
settled condition. In light of this the psalmist prays that God will

- restore us – BDB 996, KB 1427, Polel IMPERFECT, cf. Ps. 80:3,7,19;
85:4; 126:1; Lam. 5:21

- heal (i.e., "restore," NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 1163) the land – BDB 950, KB 1272,
Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. 2 Chr. 7:14; this may refer to the breach in the
wall of Ps. 60:1a

It must be stated that all of these prayer requests for God's help, protection, deliverance
are based on His people's faith and lifestyle (cf. 2 Chr. 6:37-39). All God's promises (except for the
ones connected to Messiah and His ministry) are conditional (i.e., "if. . .then").

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL
TOPIC: YHWH'S COVENANT REQUIREMENTS OF ISRAEL

60:1 The rejection by God (cf. Ps. 60:1,10) of His people (cf. Ps. 60:3,5) is shocking! We must
remember that God had a purpose for Israel. She was to be a mechanism for the worldwide revelation of
God's character and purposes (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL
REDEMPTIVE PLAN, cf. Ezek. 36:22-36). This demanded faithful covenant obedience (cf. 1 Chr. 28:9).
Because of the Fall of Genesis 3 they could not; judgment was the only option (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-30).

▣ "in His holiness" This phrase in Ps. 60:6 is a powerful reminder of the character
of God that He wants His people to emulate and model for the nations (see
SPECIAL
TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD [OT]).

A new approach was necessary. This new approach is called "the new covenant"
(cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36), which the NT clarifies as the gospel of Jesus Christ.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY ONE

▣ "You have been angry" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD, I. C. #2

▣ "O" This VOCATIVE in the NASB in line 2 refers to the name for God in line 1., "O
God," which is Elohim.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

60:2a This imagery could relate to

- YHWH coming to His creation which causes it to convulse (i.e., Jdgs. 5:4-5; Ps. 18:7; 68:8; Isa. 13:13;
Hag. 2:6)

- the second part of line 1, "split," may refer to a breach in the walls of Jerusalem allowing foreign soldiers to
enter the city (cf. 60:2b)

60:3b This is imagery of a drunk person, which was used of confusion, ineffective defense (i.e., Isa. 51:17-20 and
Jer. 25:15-29). The Bible always condemns drunkenness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WINE

SPECIAL TOPIC: CUP

60:4-5 To me this should be a separate strophe (cf. NKJV, NRSV). The SUBJECT
changes from Ps. 60:1-3. This strophe describes YHWH's actions on behalf of Israel.

- He has given those who revere Him a banner (BDB 651, i.e., a visible sign or way to
communicate, cf. Exod. 17:15; Isa. 5:26; 11:12; 13:2; Ps. 20:5); this could be a negative
(i.e., flee) or positive (i.e., rally to) expression.

- He wants it displayed to communicate Himself (i.e., the truth; the Hebrew consonants
קשׁט can mean "of the bow" or "truth," BDB 905; UBS
Text Project support "of the bow" with a "B" rating (some doubt); the
NRSV, NJB, NET Bible; REB support this choice but NKJV and JPSOA have "truth." The
word for "bow" has an added vowel only here.

The point seems to be that YHWH is providing some support to Israel by His presence with
them in battle.

60:4 "a banner" /this word (BDB 651, KB 701) has several uses.

- a national flag of military victory ‒ Ps. 20:5

- a warniang sign ‒ Num. 26:10

- a rallying place during battle

- a symbol of the inclusion of the nations (after judgment) ‒ Isa. 5:26; 11:12; 13:2

- in this context it is related to

- the covenant people's hope (i.e., YHWH's presence)

- the truth of YHWH's revelation (LXX, Peshitta, and Vulgate, cf. Pro. 22:31; the MT has "rally to it
out of bowship." UBS Text Project supports this with a "B" rating)

▣ "Selah" See notes at Ps. 3:2 and Intro. to Psalms, VII.

60:5-12 This is repeated in Ps. 108:6-13.

60:5 "Your beloved" This ADJECTIVE (BDB 391) is used of YHWH's
covenant people (cf. Isa. 5:1; Jer. 11:15; 12:7). It is a strong, passionate description.

▣ This verse has two prayer requests based on Ps. 60:4.

- save us (MT; Qere "me") – BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil
IMPERATIVE, i.e., by Your actions, cf. Ps. 3:7; 20:9

- answer us (MT, Qere "me") – BDB 772, KB 851, Qal
IMPERATIVE

The UBS Text Project (p. 277) gives the MT's "us" a "C" rating
(considerable doubt). The PLURAL is in Ps. 60:10 and 11.

▣ "Your right hand" This is a Hebrew idiom of power and effective action
(cf. Exod. 15:6; Ps. 17:7; 44:3; 98:1; 108:6; 138:7; 139:10.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

60:6-8 This strophe extols YHWH's sovereignty (or "holiness," BDB 871; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY, or possibly "in His sanctuary," JPSOA) over
the nations (cf. Deut. 32:8). These verses are repeated in Ps. 108:6-13, which means it may have
been part of temple liturgy. It may be connected to Exod. 15:14-17. YHWH Himself speaks (i.e., "God
has spoken" – BDB 180, KB 210, Piel PERFECT).

- I will exult – BDB 759, KB 831, Qal COHORTATIVE

- I will portion out – BDB 323, KB 322, Piel COHORTATIVE

- I will measure out – BDB 551, KB 547, Piel IMPERFECT used in
a COHORTATIVE sense

- "is mine"

- same as #4

- "is the helmet of My head"

- "is My scepter"

- "over I shall throw my shoe" (i.e., an idiom of contempt or ownership, cf. Ruth 4:7)

- "shout loud, because of Me" (possibly should be, "over Philistia I will
shout aloud," like Ps. 108:9c)

Notice the place names are all in the tribal allocations of Joshua 12-19.

- one city – Shechem

- one valley – valley of Succoth

- one area – Gilead

- three tribes – Manasseh, Ephraim, Judah (for Judah as scepter see Gen. 49:10)

- three defeated Canaanite nations – Moab, Edom, Philistia

9Who
will bring me into the besieged city?
Who
will lead me to Edom?
10Have
not You Yourself, O God, rejected us?
And
will You not go forth with our armies, O God?
11O give us help against
the adversary,
For
deliverance by man is in vain.
12Through
God we shall do valiantly,
And
it is He who will tread down our adversaries.

60:9-12 This strophe speaks of the impossibility of military victories without YHWH's
help and presence (i.e., Holy War).

- Ps. 60:9 asks the military question

- Ps. 60:10 asserts the spiritual reality (i.e., Holy War) that unless YHWH goes before
Israel's army, no victory is possible, cf. Ps. 44:9; 108:11

- Ps. 60:11 asserts the physical reality that military victory by humans is vain and fleeting

- Ps. 60:12 asserts that only with YHWH can there be victory, cf. Deut. 20:1; 1 Sam.17:45,47;
Ps. 20:7; 22:16-17; 44:1-3,5-7; 146:3; Zech. 4:6). This is referring to the victory of God's
purposes in Israel as a light to the nations, not just a conqueror.

The whole point of these assertions is the question of Ps. 60:10, "Have You, Yourself,
O God, rejected us?" (i.e., conditional covenant known as "the two ways," cf. Leviticus 26;
Deuteronomy 27-30; Psalm 1; the Mosaic covenant is conditional; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT). Unless He gives help there is no hope (Ps. 60:11b). If He does, there will
be victory (Ps. 60:12), both for God's purpose and Israel's security and peace.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL
REDEMPTIVE PLAN

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation.
You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of
the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Read the Psalm and try to divide it into subjects, topics. Do you think Ps. 60:1-3 and Ps. 60:4-5
are separate topics?

- What is the theological purpose of Ps. 60:6-8? Why is it repeated in Psalm 108?

- Psalm 60:8 has several negative images. Explain them.

- What is the main theological truth of Ps. 60:9-12?
